title: The Biggest Crackdown on Indian Crime in U.S. History Just Swept Three Continents. Here Is What It Means for the Diaspora.
excerpt: Operation Hard Ball charged 37 people tied to the Bishnoi and Bhagwanpuria gangs with racketeering, political assassination, and drug trafficking — and prosecutors say the investigation is far from over.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Operation Hard Ball charged 37 individuals linked to Indian crime syndicates with serious offenses.
  • The Bishnoi gang, led by Lawrence Bishnoi, orchestrated crimes from prison, including political assassinations.
  • Over 50 raids resulted in the seizure of 1,000 kg of cocaine and multiple firearms.
  • The case has heightened concerns within the Indian American community, especially in California.
  • Seven fugitives remain at large, with many facing sentences of 10 years to life if convicted.

The most sweeping law-enforcement action ever taken against India-based organised crime on American soil landed last week with the force of its name. Operation Hard Ball — a years-long investigation led by the FBI's Los Angeles field office, the LAPD, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police — resulted in three federal indictments, 37 defendants charged, and at least 24 arrests across the United States, Canada, and Europe. For the roughly five million Indian Americans and permanent residents in the United States, the case is a reckoning. It lays bare how criminal networks rooted in Punjab have stretched their operations into Bay Area suburbs, Inland Empire warehouses, and quiet Thousand Oaks neighborhoods — extorting diaspora families, trafficking narcotics, and, prosecutors allege, ordering assassinations from behind prison walls. ## Three Syndicates, One Investigation At the centre of the case is the Bishnoi enterprise, run by 33-year-old Lawrence Bishnoi from an Indian prison cell using smuggled cellphones. Despite more than a decade of incarceration, Bishnoi allegedly directed "political assassinations, murders, shootings, extortions, kidnappings, drug trafficking, human smuggling, and other crimes," according to court documents unsealed in the Central District of California. The most high-profile charge: Bishnoi and his North American lieutenant, Satinderjeet Singh — known as "Goldy Brar" — are accused of ordering the June 2023 assassination of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, a Sikh community leader gunned down outside his temple in Surrey, British Columbia. Canada designated the Bishnoi enterprise a terrorist entity in September 2025; the U.S. indictment now adds American racketeering and extortion charges. > **""Transnational criminal gangs who spread fear, drugs, and violence will face the full force of justice and the weight of the federal government," said First Assistant U.S."** The second syndicate, the Bhagwanpuria gang led by 38-year-old imprisoned gangster Jaggu Bhagwanpuria, allegedly operates a thousand-member network stretching from Punjab to California and Ohio. Prosecutors say the gang specialised in murder-for-hire, weapons trafficking, and extortion schemes that targeted families in the United States — at times colluding with corrupt Indian law enforcement to fabricate criminal charges against rivals back home. A third group, the Dhanda Drug Trafficking Organisation run from Vancouver by Ravinder Singh Dhanda — who operated under the alias "John Wick" — allegedly brokered smuggling services for bulk quantities of cocaine and methamphetamine using long-haul semi-trucks and farming vehicles on the U.S.–Canada border. ## What Was Seized ![Los Angeles — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Hollywood_Sign_%28Zuschnitt%29.jpg/3840px-Hollywood_Sign_%28Zuschnitt%29.jpg) The scale of the investigation is staggering. Agents executed more than 50 raids, seizing roughly 1,000 kilograms of cocaine, one kilogram of heroin, a dozen firearms, and $40,000 in cash. Twenty-three search warrants were served in the Sacramento area alone, with another 11 in Los Angeles. Arrests stretched from Stockton and the Bay Area to Indiana, Georgia, Spain, and multiple Canadian provinces. From March 2024 to July 2025, the Bishnoi enterprise allegedly stole more than 500 kilograms of cocaine from rival drug gangs in Los Angeles — a detail that underscores how deeply the syndicate had embedded itself in California's narcotics ecosystem. "Transnational criminal gangs who spread fear, drugs, and violence will face the full force of justice and the weight of the federal government," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli. "There is no safe harbour for these thugs."

## The Diaspora Fallout The case has sent a chill through Indian American communities, particularly in California, where the Bishnoi enterprise extorted a wealthy Thousand Oaks resident for $5 million and where members of the Bhagwanpuria gang reaped cash through drug trafficking in Los Angeles and the Inland Empire. It also rekindles the painful diplomatic wound of the Nijjar assassination, which ruptured India-Canada relations for over a year. The U.S. indictment does not accuse the Indian government of involvement — and prosecutors said Indian authorities "were cooperative in the investigation" — but the case gives fresh ammunition to Sikh advocacy groups who have long alleged that state actors stand behind the violence. "How does a gangster incarcerated inside a maximum-security Indian prison run a global cross-border assassination syndicate?" asked Sikhs for Justice, a U.S.-based advocacy organisation. "Lawrence Bishnoi is merely the proxy finger pulling the trigger."
Impact on the Indian Diaspora
›Indian American community faces increased fear of crime.
›Bishnoi gang extorted $5 million from a Thousand Oaks resident.
›Nijjar assassination has strained India-Canada relations.
›U.S. seeks extradition of Lawrence Bishnoi.
The Justice Department has signalled it will seek Bishnoi's extradition — a legally and diplomatically fraught process. Seven fugitives remain at large in the U.S., two in India, and one in Europe. If convicted, many defendants face mandatory minimum sentences of 10 years to life. For the Indian diaspora, the message from federal law enforcement is clear: the long arm of Punjab's criminal underworld no longer stops at the Indian border, and the American legal system intends to meet it head-on.
